editorial.headline: Fabric Sack Manufacturing, Open Nationally and Not Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers woven or knitted fabric sacks, with national PMA ownership open up to 100% and no Bali moratorium block in the record.
editorial.body:
Fabric sack manufacturing under code 13924 is a narrow industrial activity: making bagor sacks, including belacu sacks commonly used for flour or sugar, and other sacks made from woven or knitted fabric. Its center of gravity is textile conversion, not paper packaging and not sheet-plastic sack production. The slim record is plain on that boundary, and it matters because this is not a broad packaging label; it is a manufacturing classification for fabric sacks as a finished industrial product.

The business scale picture is unusually broad. The record opens this activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar operators, so it can describe a small production setup as well as a larger factory-scale operation. That does not mean every operator looks the same in practice, but the classification itself is not reserved only for one size of business. A founder reading this code should understand it as a textile-manufacturing activity that can be registered across the full stated scale range, from micro to large.

Nationally, the investment signal is straightforward. The PMA status is TERBUKA, and the foreign-ownership ceiling in the record is 100%. In plain English, the national classification is open to foreign ownership up to the full percentage stated in the record. The source named for that national PMA position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. There is no separate percentage to invent, no implied lower ceiling, and no additional capital threshold in this record.

The Bali side is also clean, but for a different reason. The record does not mark this activity as blocked in Bali: l4_bali_blocked is false, and the Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. The recorded reason is explicit: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium.” That matters because the Bali moratorium rule in the record blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA island-wide, permanently. Here, the record’s own Bali reasoning says the activity is not caught by that block. The honest reading is therefore simple: this code is open nationally for PMA up to 100%, and the slim record does not block PMA registration in Bali under the stated moratorium logic.
